text: Searching an unsorted list of N items classically takes, on average, order-N tries — checking items one by one. Grover's algorithm does the same job on a quantum computer in roughly order-root-N steps, and this lesson builds the smallest possible example by hand so you can see exactly how that speedup happens.

Here's a complete, minimal 2-qubit Grover circuit searching a 4-item space for the single marked item |11>, using exactly one Grover iteration. h on both qubits puts the system into equal superposition — all 4 states at probability 0.25, nothing favored yet. cz(0,1) is the oracle: it flips the sign of the amplitude on |11> only, marking the target without revealing it or changing any probability yet.

The five-gate block that follows is the diffuser, sometimes called inversion about the mean. It reflects every amplitude around the average, converting that single phase flip into a large boost in the marked state's measurement probability. Then measure reads out the result.

This specific case, 4 items with 1 marked, gives a genuinely exact result, not an approximation. After exactly one full Grover iteration, the resulting state is exactly |11> at probability 1.0, and everything else at zero. The formula for the optimal iteration count, pi-over-4 times the square root of N over M, happens to work out to exactly 1 for this case. For larger search spaces, that optimal count is a real number that gets rounded to a nearby integer, so you land close to probability 1 but not exactly at it.

Grover's diffuser-and-oracle step is a geometric rotation, and rotations are periodic — they cycle. Running more iterations past the optimal count doesn't keep improving your odds; it rotates the state past the marked outcome and back toward the unmarked ones. For real search problems, qiskit_algorithms provides Grover and AmplificationProblem, which take your oracle and automatically build the matching diffuser and figure out the iteration count — exactly what you just built by hand, generalized.
Next lesson covers a different kind of building block entirely: the Quantum Fourier Transform, the subroutine hiding inside Shor's algorithm and quantum phase estimation.
